title: The state of genetic literacy among high school students in Czechia
content:
by Marek Procházka, Markéta Klimešová, Vanda Janštová

To investigate high school students’ understanding of modern genetics and to characterize the obstacles that impede deeper understanding of this subject, we translated the Learning Progression‑Based Assessment of Modern Genetics diagnostic instrument into Czech and validated it with 282 Czech high school students. We present the Czech version of this instrument which spans Mendelian genetics; molecular biology (proteins, nucleic acids, gene expression); mutation; cell division; genetics–evolution connections; environmental influences on phenotype; intra‑individual and inter‑individual genetic variation; and interspecific differences. Czech high school students frequently fail to connect proteins to phenotypic traits, rarely attain molecular‑level reasoning, and underappreciate the evolutionary significance of genetic mechanisms. Higher performance was associated with participation in biology seminars and science competitions, perceived importance of genetics, and intentions for biology‑related tertiary study. Aligning with original US validation data, Czech high school students demonstrated strong procedural proficiency in traditional Mendelian genetics but experienced difficulties with advanced concepts like gene regulation, epigenetics, and evolutionary mutations. Although a specific conceptual bottleneck emerged in Czech students’ ability to bridge classical and molecular genetics, the overall consistency between cohorts highlights that advanced mechanistic reasoning remains a persistent barrier across contexts. Our study identifies targets for instructional improvement, including greater emphasis on protein.
